title: Your first day in Nova
description: A practical route from your first login to a team you understand.
sections: Follow the opening path

Start with the opening story and the in-game tutorial. Try each newly introduced control before moving on: understanding when you are attacking, moving, or activating a skill is more useful than copying an advanced setup immediately. Continue until the game has introduced the systems you want to use; unlock conditions should always be checked in your current client.
Choose a small first goal

Pick one manageable objective for the session: finish the next story stage, learn a Trekker, or clear content that is blocking your progress. If you fail, identify the actual problem before spending materials. Were you taking avoidable damage, missing skill timings, or running out of damage? Those problems need different solutions.
Build a core, then expand

Start with a small group of Trekkers you enjoy using. Read their current skill descriptions and decide which character your team is built around. Spend only enough to test that idea before committing scarce resources. A broader collection becomes useful when you understand what each new addition changes.
Keep a simple notebook

After a run, note the team, the content, and one thing you would change. This gives you a way to compare attempts without relying on memory. Use the character directory to keep favorite Trekkers close at hand, then read the team-building guide when you are ready to refine your group.

title: Build your first team
description: Start with a plan, connect your skills, and test one change at a time.
sections: Give the team a purpose

Choose the content you want to clear before choosing the characters. A team for comfortable progression may have different priorities from one designed to improve a clear time. Decide which Trekker is central to the plan, and read what their damage or utility depends on.
Read the conditions, not just the numbers

For each candidate teammate, look at who receives the effect, what triggers it, how long it lasts, and whether it is available when you need it. Matching elements can help you discover candidates, but shared element alone does not prove synergy. Verify interactions in the current skill text.
Test on repeatable content

Use the same stage or encounter for comparisons. Change one slot or one upgrade at a time, then observe both clear speed and reliability. A setup that finishes once but fails repeatedly is different from one you can use comfortably every session.
Keep alternatives for specific problems

When the core team works, make a short list of replacements for situations it struggles with. Avoid upgrading every alternative in advance. First confirm that the replacement solves a real problem and that the materials needed are worth the improvement.

title: Before you enter a Monolith
description: Prepare with intention, read your choices, and learn from each attempt.
sections: Set a run objective

Monoliths are a central part of exploring Nova. Before entering, decide whether you are progressing, learning an encounter, or testing a setup. Read the conditions displayed in the game rather than assuming a previous run uses the same rules.
Check the team before committing

Review your selected Trekkers and the upgrades already available to them. Make sure you can explain what each slot contributes. If the team depends on a particular effect, check its requirements before relying on it during a run.
Make choices that support the plan

When the run offers a choice, read the full effect. Prefer a coherent set of interactions over unrelated bonuses that merely look large. If you are experimenting, change one part of the plan so the result tells you something useful.
Review the bottleneck

After the attempt, identify where the plan broke down. Separate execution problems from preparation problems: learning an attack pattern does not require the same response as improving a neglected upgrade. Make one targeted adjustment before trying again.

title: Spend with a plan
description: A calm approach to upgrades, limited materials, and long-term goals.
sections: Separate needs from experiments

Before using a scarce material, name the improvement you expect. Is this required to clear a stage, a useful investment in your core team, or just an interesting experiment? All three can be valid, but they should not compete blindly for the same resources.
Prioritize the next useful upgrade

Inspect the materials and benefits of the next upgrade in the game. Compare it with other unfinished improvements on the team. Avoid spreading resources across a large roster when one focused improvement would remove your current bottleneck.
Keep a reserve for decisions

If you are unsure about a character or a future plan, waiting is a legitimate choice. Do not assume a guide from an older version reflects the current game. Confirm costs and conditions in the client before committing limited resources.
Review your plan weekly

Your priorities change as new content opens and your collection grows. Revisit the core team and the content you enjoy. A resource plan is useful when it supports your goals, not when it forces you to keep investing in a direction you no longer want.

title: Navigate the six elements
description: Use element filters to explore options without confusing similarity with synergy.
sections: Learn the directory labels

The roster uses six element labels: Ignis, Aqua, Ventus, Terra, Lux, and Umbra. The character directory lets you filter these groups and combine them with rarity or name searches. This is an efficient first step when looking for alternatives.
Treat filters as discovery tools

Two Trekkers sharing an element do not automatically share a role, trigger, or play pattern. Open their individual entries, then compare the actual skill conditions in game. An element filter narrows the search; it does not finish the team-building decision.
Keep alternate forms separate

A named variant should be treated as its own roster entry. For example, Noya and Firstlight Noya have separate pages and different element and rarity labels. Search the full name so that you do not apply information from the wrong form.
Move from shortlist to testing

Save a few candidates, choose a specific piece of content, and compare them one at a time. Record which interaction you expected and whether it happened. Use the team-building guide for a repeatable testing process.

title: How to read a tier list
description: Understand the assumptions behind a rank before using it to spend resources.
sections: Ask what the ranking measures

A rank is only meaningful with a context. Check the version, content, investment level, and team assumptions behind it. A ranking for optimized clears may not answer which character feels best for a new account.
Separate strength from account value

Even a strong Trekker may add little if you cannot support the setup it requires. Conversely, a less highly ranked option can solve a specific problem in your current collection. Consider what changes for your account instead of looking at the letter alone.
Use the Atlas board intentionally

The Atlas tier list is a personal planning board, not a verified meta ranking. Assign your own S, A, or B labels, or leave a character unranked. Define what those labels mean for your goal, such as favorite playstyle or next investment priority.
Revisit your assumptions

If a team changes or you try new content, update the board. Keep notes about why you moved a character. Browser-local storage preserves this board on the same browser, but it does not synchronize automatically between devices.

title: A routine that fits your time
description: Keep your sessions focused without turning the game into a second job.
sections: Start with the current notices

Check the in-game notices and official news for active events, deadlines, and eligibility. Date-sensitive instructions can change, so avoid relying on an old screenshot or a guide written for a previous version.
Choose your session size

For a short session, focus on the most relevant tasks for your current goal. For a longer one, add story progression or a team experiment. Decide how much time you want to spend before beginning rather than trying to complete everything by default.
Group similar tasks

Look at the tasks currently available in your client and identify which ones overlap. Where possible, work toward the same goal with the same team. Do not spend resources solely to finish a low-value task without comparing the cost to the reward.
Finish with one next step

Leave yourself a simple note: the next stage to try, material to collect, or teammate to test. A clear next step makes returning easier and helps you avoid spending the first part of every session deciding what to do.

title: Choose your next Trekker investment
description: Turn a long character wishlist into a short, useful priority list.
sections: Start from your existing collection

List the Trekkers you already use and the content you are struggling with. Identify the gap you actually need to fill before browsing new options. Rarity is a useful collection label, but it is not a complete explanation of value.
Compare the whole cost

Look beyond the initial acquisition or first upgrade. Consider the resources required to make the candidate useful alongside the rest of your team. Verify exact costs in the current client; Atlas does not supply version-specific material totals.
Test what you can before committing

If the game offers a way to try a character or inspect its skills, use it. Check whether you enjoy the play pattern as well as whether it solves the intended problem. A theoretical improvement is less valuable if you do not enjoy using it.
Rank priorities, then revisit

Use the personal tier board as a shortlist. Keep only a few immediate priorities, and leave uncertain options unranked. Revisit the list when your goals change instead of treating the initial decision as permanent.
